conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been feeling really nauseous and vomiting for the past day. It’s similar to what I’ve had before with my stomach not emptying right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see you have a history of gastroparesis. Any abdominal pain or back pain with this episode?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little lower back pain, but not too bad. My stomach is bloated, and I’m only throwing up small amounts. I haven’t had fevers though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also see your blood sugar was very high when you arrived—699. That can definitely make gastroparesis worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s not good. I’ve been struggling to keep it under control. Did you give me insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you got 10 units IV when you arrived and another 8 units later. We’ll keep monitoring it and adjust your insulin while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My right wrist feels better, by the way. The pain’s much improved since last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. The ortho team checked it and said the wound is healing well. No signs of infection now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my hip? That’s not bothering me at all anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, your hip pain has resolved. You’re walking fine, which is great. We’ll keep focusing on your stomach and blood sugar for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been having black stools. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s something we need to watch. It could be from old blood, possibly related to gastritis or your recent C. diff. We’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not having any bright red blood, just these loose, dark ones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That helps. No hematochezia is reassuring. We’ll keep you on bowel rest for now and give you IV fluids and meds to help with nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m just glad I’m not in pain like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood work from yesterday showed your sodium was low—123. That’s likely due to fluid overload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? I’ve had low sodium before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially with your other conditions. We think the extra fluid in your body—about 7 kg over your dry weight—is part of what triggered this flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why my stomach feels so bloated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Fluid can cause swelling in the bowel, making it harder to move food through. That’s why we’re doing dialysis today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I forgot I was scheduled for HD. Will that help me feel better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, removing the extra fluid should reduce the bloating and help your stomach start working better. You’ll have another session tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. What about my antibiotics? I’m still on cefazolin and the vancomycin lock, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re still on IV cefazolin twice a week after dialysis, and the vancomycin lock in your portacath every 48 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And metronidazole for C. diff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re continuing that three times a day until the full course is done, which lines up with finishing the cefazolin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want that coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling after dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Actually, I feel a bit better. My stomach doesn’t feel as full.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’re also seeing your sodium improve—from 123 to 135. Your blood sugar is still high but coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that good progress?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And your latest blood culture showed no growth, which means no active bloodstream infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So the antibiotics are working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They are. We’ll keep you on them as planned. Once the vancomycin locks are done, you’ll go back to heparin locks in your port.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. You’ve tolerated a full breakfast, and your symptoms have improved a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I actually ate all my eggs. I haven’t been able to do that in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. Your labs this morning show your kidney function and sodium are much better. We think you’re ready to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your meds, especially insulin, cefazolin, metronidazole, and the vancomycin locks. And try to limit fluids to 2 liters a day to prevent this from happening again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best. And I’ll follow up with my diabetes doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and OPAT will manage your antibiotics. Call your mom to let her know you’re going home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she’s my contact. I’ll call her right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. We’ll discharge you later this morning. No need for ortho follow-up unless your wrist or hip starts bothering you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.
